name: Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Histopathological Diagnostic Criteria for Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis

criteria.description: Presence of linear and whorled hyperpigmented macules following the lines of Blaschko
Onset of pigmentation within the first two years of life, typically at birth or early infancy
Skin biopsy showing increased basal layer melanin without melanocyte proliferation or pigment incontinence
Lack of preceding inflammatory or vesicular skin lesions
No systemic abnormalities or developmental delay

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of characteristic linear and whorled hyperpigmentation with onset in early infancy plus supportive histopathological findings
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by histopathology; genetic testing is not routinely diagnostic.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Linear and whorled hyperpigmented macules following Blaschko's lines
searchTerms: linear and swirled dark skin patches
gradual darkening of skin without rash
dark skin patches sparing mouth and genitals

common.symptomName: Absence of pruritus or pain in affected skin
searchTerms: no itching or pain in pigmented skin

common.symptomName: Stable or slowly progressive pigmentation over time
searchTerms: stable or slowly worsening skin color changes

occasional.symptomName: Mild hypopigmented streaks adjacent to hyperpigmented areas
searchTerms: light skin streaks next to dark patches
pale streaks near dark skin areas

laboratory: Skin biopsy showing increased basal layer melanin without melanocyte proliferation
imaging: Skeletal X-rays if musculoskeletal anomalies suspected
Brain MRI if neurological symptoms present
genetic: Postzygotic mosaicism suspected but no consistent genetic mutation identified
other: Clinical observation of pigmentation pattern along Blaschko's lines

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of inflammatory vesicular lesions in early stages
Systemic involvement including dental and ocular abnormalities
Often associated with neurological and musculoskeletal abnormalities
Pigmentation follows Blaschko's lines but is lighter than surrounding skin
Possible systemic involvement including neurological and skeletal abnormalities

redFlags: Rapid progression of pigmentation with ulceration or inflammation
Neurological deficits such as seizures or developmental delay
Presence of systemic abnormalities (cardiac, skeletal, ocular)
